# Results — Study 499 (Trendline-Break)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
confirmed close below the rising trendline breaks support and forecasts a turn down** — encoded
as a mechanical rule. Swing lows are confirmed fractals (k = 10, with a 10-bar confirmation
lag); at every bar a rising trendline is least-squares-fit through the three latest confirmed
lows; a signal fires on the first close below that line, entered at the **next close** (one
documented lag). The folklore is bearish, so returns are **sign-flipped (a short)**: a positive
number = the break correctly forecast a drop. We measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return on
SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py`
to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **617** mechanical trendline breaks pooled across the 5 tapes (k = 10, 3-low OLS fit) |
| Timing / costs | confirmed-fractal swing lows usable only **+10 bars** later; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per break |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — break-short vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (here it merely measures that a *short* fights the
index's upward drift); the **Welch break-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = break − random.

| horizon | n | break (short) | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (break−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 617 | −34.8 bps  | 41% | −3.75 | −14.8 bps  | **−20.0 bps**  | −36.8 bps  | −1.45 | 0.148 |
| 10-day | 615 | −63.8 bps  | 39% | −4.30 | −16.6 bps  | **−47.2 bps**  | −65.8 bps  | −2.43 | 0.015 |
| 20-day | 614 | −105.6 bps | 36% | −4.36 | −53.0 bps  | **−52.6 bps**  | −107.6 bps | −1.92 | 0.055 |
| 60-day | 611 | −317.5 bps | 27% | −7.05 | −191.5 bps | **−126.0 bps** | −319.5 bps | −2.84 | 0.005 |

Read it carefully. The break-short loses money at **every** horizon, and it loses *more* than a
drift-matched random short — Δ is negative at all four horizons and the Welch *t* is **negative**
(down to −2.84 at 60 days). The folklore's "support broke, it falls" is exactly backwards on
this tape: a close below the rising trendline is, on average, a **fresh local low that bounces
up** (a false breakdown / bear trap), so shorting it bleeds. The break does **not** beat random
in the bearish direction it was sold for — the only honest reading is **no signal**.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the break-short loses to random in all 5 names

| ticker | entries | break (short) | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (break−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 128 | −117.8 bps | −2.27 | −53.8 bps  | **−63.9 bps** |
| QQQ | 114 | −140.3 bps | −2.48 | −102.3 bps | **−38.0 bps** |
| IWM | 122 | −118.6 bps | −1.87 | −15.1 bps  | **−103.5 bps** |
| DIA | 132 | −39.6 bps  | −0.92 | −24.4 bps  | **−15.2 bps** |
| GLD | 121 | −119.2 bps | −2.24 | −75.4 bps  | **−43.9 bps** |

In **5 of 5** names the famous break *underperforms* a dart-throwing short. No coherent
cross-sectional edge — and the negative sign is consistent everywhere: the break marks a
bounce, not a breakdown.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the slope, nothing changes

The decisive "does the geometry matter?" test: keep the swing-low **positions** and the price
**marginal**, but permute which price sits at which low, so the fitted trendline's slope/level
become geometric nonsense. If price genuinely respected *this specific line*, the scramble would
collapse the result.

| test | observed break-short 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-slope trendline | −117.8 bps | **0.631** | 500 |

**63% of scrambled-slope trendlines match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.631). The specific
least-squares line carries no information — geometric nonsense does just as well. "The break
forecasts a turn" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real post-break effect

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-break **bounce** (knob `edge`), the same break
detector — read as a **fade** (long the breakdown, `short=False`, the direction the geometry can
actually bank) — behaves exactly as it must. So the flat/adverse real-tape result is a genuine
"the folklore is wrong", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | fade (long) | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 83 | +3.6 bps   | 48% | +0.05 |
| **0.40** (real planted bounce) | 49 | +734.7 bps | 92% | **+9.01** |

With no planted bounce the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted bounce
lights up at *t* = +9.01 with a 92% win-rate. The detector is live — and it tells us the
bankable conditional effect at a break point is *reversion up*, the exact opposite of the
folklore's *short*.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The trendline-break **short** (the folklore tradable) does **not** beat a
  drift-matched random baseline — it is *significantly worse* (Δ = −20.0 / −47.2 / −52.6 /
  −126.0 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; Welch *t* negative throughout, down to −2.84 at 60 days).
  The break "forecasts" the opposite of what it claims: it marks a bounce, not a breakdown.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no tradable edge in the bearish direction the rule was
  sold for; the break-short bleeds, and costs only deepen the hole. (The mirror — *fading* the
  break long — merely re-buys the index's drift you already own; the placebo shows the line
  itself adds nothing either way.)
- **"Does the trendline break forecast?" — BUSTED.** The shuffled-slope placebo leaves the
  result intact (*p* = 0.631): geometric-nonsense trendlines do as well as the real ones, so the
  specific least-squares support line carries no forecasting information. The trendline break is
  a descriptive drawing artefact, not a forecasting signal.
